claims.text: A tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy can be engineered with stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations.
A tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy with SCCPs can exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition with increasing temperature.
The SCCP tungsten refractory high-entropy alloy is ductile at room temperature.
The alloy becomes brittle within a narrow intermediate-temperature window.
The alloy recovers ductility at still higher temperatures.
The initial microstructure consists of coherent nanoprecipitates within a continuous matrix.
Temperature ramping during mechanical testing can be used to probe the alloy's mechanical behavior across temperature ranges.
Dislocation behavior and nanoprecipitate morphology can change within the tested intermediate-temperature window.
Coherent nanoprecipitates and their interfaces are the structural mediators of the proposed transition.
At low temperatures, dislocation slip in the continuous matrix provides ductility.
In the intermediate-temperature range, coherent interfaces restrict dislocation movement.
Stress concentration at coherent interfaces induces the intermediate-temperature brittle response.
At higher temperatures, increased dislocation activity and twinning become active and restore ductility.
Conventional tungsten alloys typically undergo monotonic ductility loss when approaching temper embrittlement and do not recover at high temperature.
The ductile–brittle–ductile behavior requires a stable SCCP microstructure and effective coherent interfaces.
Coherent SCCP interfaces relieve stress concentrations.
Excessive nanoprecipitate coarsening or interface degradation may eliminate the transition.
The exact temperature range of the brittle window is not specified.
The transition temperatures and quantitative ductility changes depend on the alloy composition and processing history.
Failure to observe a measurable intermediate-temperature ductility drop would falsify the proposed transition.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says coherent interfaces generate stress concentrations and restrict dislocations, whereas the boundary describes the same interfaces as stress relievers. The cited evidence supports stress relief and facilitated dislocation transmission, not the proposed embrittling action.
